The receptionist asks which visit she means, and Maya gives the approximate date and clinician’s name. Maya asks how she will receive an update and confirms the contact details on file. stories.brief: At a busy neighborhood café, friends Liat and Niv order several dishes to share before heading to work. When the server brings the food, they realize one friend has to leave early and ask whether the bill can be divided between them. The server explains that it is easier to separate the drinks from the shared dishes, so Liat asks whether they can pay for their own drinks and split the rest. Niv checks that this works for him, and the server confirms the arrangement before bringing the card terminal. They pay without holding up the next customers, and Niv takes the remaining food in a container they ask for at the counter.

translations.en: that they will split it that way

stories.brief: On a free morning, friends Yael and Amir arrive at a lakeside activity center for a guided kayak session. They ask the instructor what to do with their bags and whether they will be in the same kayak. The instructor explains the available setup and shows them how to adjust their life vests; Amir says his feels loose, so they check the fit again together. Before setting off, Yael asks how to signal if they want to pause, and the instructor demonstrates. They paddle along the sheltered shore, stop to watch birds near the reeds, and return to shore having completed the short route. They collect their belongings and agree that next time they would like to stay on the water a little longer.

stories.brief: Fully AI-generated dialogue. In a neighborhood postal branch, Gil wants to send a small ceramic bowl to his sister and asks clerk Roni how to protect it in the parcel. Roni asks whether the bowl is already wrapped, and Gil explains that he has brought it in a towel but has not packed a box. Gil asks whether the branch has suitable packing materials; Roni clarifies what is available and explains how to keep the bowl from moving inside the box. Gil checks whether he should leave space around it and asks how to mark the parcel as fragile. Roni answers his questions and clarifies that the label does not replace careful packing. Gil wraps the bowl with the materials he chooses, checks that it no longer shifts, and asks what to do next. Roni explains the next step at the counter, and Gil leaves with the parcel accepted and a clear understanding of how it was packed.
A collection of independent short practical situations from ordinary daily life.

shortItems.brief: Mira notices that one letter of her name is wrong on a form she is preparing to submit. She asks the service desk which instructions explain how to correct it, and the clerk points her to the relevant section so she can check what to do before sending it.

Leah calls her clinic about a cough that has recently started and asks what details would be useful to share. The receptionist suggests noting when it began and what she has observed, then directs her to the clinician for personal medical advice.

Sam is unsure whether a household bill was paid after finding an unclear entry in the account. He asks the provider how to verify the payment, and the representative explains which reference details to compare on the bill and account record.

Before asking about a minor household claim, Dina wants to understand a term she sees in her insurance paperwork. She asks the representative where the policy explains it, and the representative directs her to the written terms so she can review them without assuming what her cover includes.

At a supermarket, Rafi picks up loose apples but cannot find the weighing scale. He asks a staff member where to weigh them, and she points out the nearby produce scale so he can print a label before paying.

Neta sees that an online order has a delivery preference she can no longer use and asks customer service how to change it. The representative directs her to the order settings, and Neta updates the preference there.

At a bus stop, Yoni realizes he is unsure how to pay for the ride and asks the driver whether contactless payment is available. The driver points him to the information displayed by the entrance, and Yoni checks it before boarding.

A parent finds a completed permission slip in a child’s school bag but is not sure where it should go. She asks the school office, and a staff member tells her which class tray to use; she leaves the slip there.

While unpacking groceries, Ido asks his housemate how to keep fresh basil for tomorrow’s meal. His housemate suggests putting the stems in a glass with a little water, so Ido sets the basil on the kitchen counter.

At a railway station, Salma checks the departure board but cannot tell which platform serves the town she plans to visit for the day. She asks an information worker, who points her to the platform listed for that destination, and she follows the signs.

When a resident’s household waste bin breaks, she asks the municipal service desk how to request a replacement. The clerk points her to the service-request form and explains which address and bin details to include, so she fills them in and submits the request.

stories.brief: Israeli fashion in the 1960s grew through local labels, factories, fashion weeks, and prominent visiting designers; the decade’s newsreels document shows and the industry’s wider reach.

sources.title: The Swinging Sixties? – Israeli Fashion in the 60s

storyBeats: In the 1960s, Israeli fashion included both local fashion houses and factories producing garments and textiles; the Israeli Film Archive describes the decade as a high point for the industry.
Local labels included Beged Or, Gottex, Maskit, and Rikma, which sold designs in Israel and found commercial success in international markets.
The first Israeli Fashion Week took place at Tel Aviv’s Sheraton Hotel in March 1965, organized with the Israel Export Institute, the Trade Fair Company, and the Department of Industry and Commerce.
More than 50 local traders and manufacturers presented their work to over 250 foreign buyers from American, European, and Japanese stores and fashion businesses.
The Export Institute reported that orders for Israeli fashion products following the 1965 event totaled about $2.5 million.
In 1961, Italian fashion houses Mingolini-Guggenheim and Schuberth sent designers and models to Israel for seven shows in one week; proceeds went to the WIZO Children’s Fund.
In 1966, a Pierre Cardin delegation presented a show at the Israel Museum; two years later, a Givenchy show used the aisles of Tel Aviv’s Culture Palace as its runway.

Maskit, which had begun as a government-supported enterprise, shifted toward lower-cost mass production in 1960; the lower-priced collection followed financial problems and surplus stock, and the company was sold to private owners in 1964.
The Diva swimwear factory, founded in 1942 by the Hirschthal brothers, employed more than 100 people in Tel Aviv by the 1960s, and about 80 percent of its output was earmarked for export.

A 1973 Israel Film Service documentary presented factories, industry workers, fashion products, scientific and academic involvement, and quality-control bodies as parts of the textile and fashion sector.

stories.brief: Archival films, advertisements, and newsreels from the 1920s through the 1970s show how food, eating, and citrus exports became part of efforts to shape Israeli identity and everyday life.

sources.title: More Than Just Food: Shaping a National Identity Through Cuisine

sources.publisher: Tel Aviv University, Mandate Palestine: Trademark and Patent Registries
sources.title: Jaffa Oranges
Consuming Palestine: Palestine and Palestinians in Israeli food culture

storyBeats: In the first half of the twentieth century, Zionist organizations’ nutrition advisers published Hebrew cookbooks encouraging immigrants to use locally grown fruit and vegetables, some unfamiliar to newcomers.
Newsreels recorded work in orchards and dairy farms and the growth of food manufacturing, which became associated with local production and pioneer labor.
On kibbutzim, the communal dining room was also a meeting place for assemblies, entertainment, and listening to or watching news; members ate there several times a day.

The Shamouti orange, also called the Jaffa orange, was identified in Jaffa’s orchards in the mid-nineteenth century as a mutation of the local Baladi orange; its shape, taste, peel, and relative lack of seeds suited it to trade.
During the Mandate, growers sent citrus through Jaffa and later Haifa ports; fruit was individually wrapped in thin paper and packed in wooden crates for export.
The words “JAFFA ORANGES” functioned as a widely used collective export brand, but were not a registered trademark and were open for different growers and traders to use.

In the 1930s, citrus was Palestine’s leading agricultural export; an account in Nature reported that the trade had recovered after wartime disruption and that Jaffa was a major exporter of grapefruit and oranges.

From 1949 to 1959, Israeli food austerity used ration books and points to distribute limited supplies; meat was rationed monthly, and some groups, including pregnant people and the ill, received additional provisions.

Shortages led families to adapt familiar recipes: the archive describes butter and oils being replaced by margarine or lower-grade plant oil, and kerosene burners becoming part of the preparation of some Iraqi and Kurdish Jewish dishes.

After austerity ended, restaurants and street diners became more visible in the 1960s and 1970s, while discussions of a shared cuisine continued amid Israel’s different cultural and ethnic traditions.

stories.brief: Israeli filmmaker and producer Micha Shagrir made hundreds of films and television works over five decades, portraying varied parts of Israeli society, including daily life and culture.
storyBeats: Micha Shagrir (1937–2015) was an Israeli director and producer whose work across five decades included hundreds of documentaries, narrative films, television series, news features, advertisements, and election broadcasts.
Born in Linz, Austria, Shagrir came to Palestine with his parents; the family lived at Kibbutz Hephzibah before moving to Tel Aviv in 1943.
As a young adult, Shagrir edited and reported for kibbutz newspapers, then worked for Israel Radio and as a field reporter and correspondent for Army Radio.
After attending a BBC television program for producers in London in 1964, Shagrir took part in establishing Israeli Television in 1967.

From 1968 to 1988, Shagrir and Dan Arazi ran Castel Communications, then one of Israel’s largest production companies; it produced documentaries, commercials, and narrative films and employed young filmmakers.

Shagrir’s subjects included Holocaust survivors, war victims and veterans, Jewish communities from Africa and the Middle East, and Ethiopian Jews; the archive notes his attention to people and places outside Israel’s social and geographic centers.
In The Elhadad Family (1980), Shagrir focused on a Moroccan Jewish family in a southern Negev development town; in 1992, he returned to the family in a sequel.
Shagrir-produced footage documented Ethiopian Jewish immigration, including Operation Moses in 1984–85 and Operation Solomon in 1991.
In Diary of an Egyptian Soldier (1979), Shagrir traveled to Alexandria to return a fallen Egyptian soldier’s diary to his parents and filmed their meeting.
His work also crossed between documentary and narrative film: he produced Avanti Popolo (1986), directed by Rafi Bukai, about Egyptian soldiers stranded in the desert after the 1967 war.
In 1980, Shagrir established a film fund in memory of his wife, editor Aliza Shagrir, to support young filmmakers; the archive says it operated for 35 years.
